summary: This work experimentally and numerically investigates how shunt resistance controls the resistive state of superconducting NbTiN wires (20 nm thick, 10 μm wide), revealing two distinct dynamic regimes: hot-spot and phase-slip behavior accessed through shunt-dependent current redistribution. Time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau simulations show that higher shunt resistance ($R_s 	o 10 \\\\\ f{R}_{\\mathrm{GL}}$) accelerates the characteristic timescale $\tau = L_K/(R_s + R_w)$ for Cooper-pair destruction/recovery cycles, transitioning the system from periodic hot-spot formation to stabilized quasi-phase-slip lines at smaller currents.
motivation: Shunts are ubiquitous in superconducting circuits for damping, protection, and current diversion, particularly in superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors where they enable sensor relaxation between detection events. Understanding how shunt resistance controls vortex dynamics in the resistive regime below the critical current has implications for optimizing current capacity and heating in these devices.
method: NbTiN whiskers with $T_c \approx 11$ K were biased with 450 ns voltage pulses to measure temperature-dependent $I$–$V$ curves across shunt resistances $R_{sh} \in \{0.03, 0.05, 0.075, 1.3\}$ Ω at $T = 5$–$9$ K. Simulations solved the TDGL equation coupled to circuit Poisson equation with $\gamma = 10$ on a $100\xi \times 100\xi$ domain, incorporating dynamic current redistribution via equation $L_K \frac{dJ_s}{dt} = (J - J_s) R_s - V_s$.
result: Measured and simulated $I$–$V$ characteristics show voltage increasing with $R_s$ at fixed current, with negative differential resistance at the hot-spot to phase-slip transition; increasing $R_s$ from $0.5$ to $10 \ R_{\\mathrm{GL}}$ reduces the destruction/recovery timescale from $\Delta t = 4929 \tau_{\\mathrm{GL}}$ to $991 \tau_{\\mathrm{GL}}$, pushing quasi-phase-slip-line formation to lower currents and lowering transition voltage by roughly an order of magnitude.
